developer setup

Set it up once. Then open a shell.

Download pkgcache and point it at your team’s server with one command. From then on pkgcache shell opens a shell in this terminal with your package tools already using the cache. Type exit and the terminal is exactly as it was.

Just the commands Explain each one

No sudo, no CA installation, no cache IP, no insecure TLS flag.

while the shell is open

Your commands, top to bottom.

Pick your platform and run the column. Every address, project and fingerprint is already this server’s own. Everything below this section is the same steps with the reasons attached.

This page is served by pkgcache, on this machine.

The cache is already here, so there is nothing to download: pkgcache shell opens a shell that uses it, pkgcache run -- npm ci runs one command through it, and pkgcache persist keeps its settings after the shell closes. The columns below also point it at your team’s server. That server’s address and fingerprint are placeholders here; its own /tutorial page shows the commands with both filled in.

first, for every platform

Download pkgcache

Choose your build5 platforms

Linux

The Docker daemon shares your loopback, so nothing here involves a certificate or a daemon setting.

  1. Name it and make it runnable

    mv pkgcache-linux-* pkgcache chmod +x pkgcache

  2. Point it at the server, once

    ./pkgcache setup -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -team-project global -limit 25G

    Checks the server’s CA against the fingerprint and keeps up to 25 GB on this machine.

  3. Open the shell

    ./pkgcache shell

    pkgcache: session ready means you are in. exit leaves it; next time this is the only command.

  4. Install packages as usual

    python -m pip install six uv pip install six npm install left-pad go mod download sudo apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$PKGCACHE_APT_PROXY" update

  5. Pull images

    ./pkgcache pull alpine:3.20

    The image keeps its own name: alpine:3.20, not a cache address.

  6. Build images

    ./pkgcache build -t myapp:dev . ./pkgcache compose build

    Your Dockerfile is never modified. Add -print to see what it would build.

macOS

Docker Desktop runs in a VM that cannot see your loopback, so Docker is told about the cache once.

  1. Name it and make it runnable

    mv pkgcache-darwin-* pkgcache chmod +x pkgcache

  2. Point it at the server, once

    ./pkgcache setup -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -team-project global -limit 25G

  3. Open the shell

    ./pkgcache shell

  4. Install packages as usual

    python -m pip install six uv pip install six npm install left-pad go mod download

  5. Teach Docker the cache, once

    ./pkgcache docker-setup

    No sudo. Restart Docker Desktop afterwards.

  6. Pull images

    ./pkgcache pull alpine:3.20

  7. Build images

    ./pkgcache build -t myapp:dev . ./pkgcache compose build

    Both reach the cache at host.docker.internal on their own, over plain HTTP — no certificate goes into a build.

Windows

PowerShell, and the same Docker Desktop step as macOS.

  1. Rename it

    Rename-Item pkgcache-windows-amd64.exe pkgcache.exe

    There is no chmod step.

  2. Point it at the server, once

    .\pkgcache.exe setup -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -team-project global -limit 25G

    A normal window is enough; Administrator is not needed for any of this column.

  3. Open the shell

    .\pkgcache.exe shell

  4. Install packages as usual

    python -m pip install six uv pip install six npm install left-pad go mod download

  5. Teach Docker the cache, once

    .\pkgcache.exe docker-setup

    Restart Docker Desktop afterwards.

  6. Pull images

    .\pkgcache.exe pull alpine:3.20

  7. Build images

    .\pkgcache.exe build -t myapp:dev .

    Working in WSL2? Use the Linux column there, with its own copy of pkgcache — a Windows program’s loopback is not the Linux one’s.

that is the whole setup

Something failed, or you want to know why any of it is shaped this way? Start walks the same steps slowly, Docker covers builders and CI, and Troubleshooting lists the errors by message.

the first three steps, in full · about two minutes

Download pkgcache, point it at the server, open a shell.

Every command on this page is already filled in for this server and for project global — the addresses and the fingerprint below are this instance’s own, not examples. If your team uses a different project, open Console → Connect and copy the command shown there instead.

You are reading this on a machine that already runs pkgcache, so step 1 is done. Steps 2 and 3 point it at your team’s server: ask the operator for that server’s address and fingerprint, or open its own /tutorial, where the commands arrive with both filled in. Without a server, step 3 works as it is — the cache then fetches from the public registries itself.

This server is not serving TLS, so no machine can be pointed at it yet.

pkgcache setup only accepts an https:// server: it fetches the CA over one unverified request, pins it to the fingerprint, and verifies everything after that. Against an http:// address it stops with server must use https. Nothing you can pass on the command line changes this, and no insecure flag is the answer.

The operator fixes it on the server host: pkgreg init mints the certificate pair into the data directory, and a server started against that data directory picks it up on restart. pkgreg doctor reports the missing pair as a failure.

  1. 1

    Download pkgcache

    One executable, not an installer. Most Intel and AMD machines are amd64; Apple silicon is darwin arm64.

    served by this server

    pkgcache downloads

    checking

    Looking for published pkgcache builds…

    Linux or macOS

    Name it pkgcache, make it executable, and check it arrived intact — the expected digest is printed under each download button above.

    mv pkgcache-linux-* pkgcache # pkgcache-darwin-* on macOS chmod +x pkgcache sha256sum pkgcache # shasum -a 256 on macOS

    Windows

    Rename it to pkgcache.exe, then check the digest. A normal PowerShell window is enough; Administrator is not needed.

    Rename-Item pkgcache-windows-amd64.exe pkgcache.exe Get-FileHash .\pkgcache.exe -Algorithm SHA256
  2. 2

    Check the fingerprint, then point pkgcache at the server

    This is the SHA-256 of the server’s public certificate authority. Compare it with the value your operator gave you through a separate trusted channel — a chat message, a wiki page, anything that is not this page. That comparison is what makes the connection safe; setup refuses to continue if it does not match.

    CA SHA-256 · the team’s server Open Console → Connect to copy the fingerprint
    Linux and macOS
    ./pkgcache setup -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -team-project global -limit 25G
    Windows PowerShell
    .\pkgcache.exe setup -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -team-project global -limit 25G

    Run it once per machine. It keeps the verified CA and the server’s address in pkgcache’s own directory and writes nothing anywhere else. -limit is how much disk the cache on this machine may use; it is asked for rather than guessed, and pkgcache limit changes it later. -team-project names the project on the server’s side.

    If your project requires an access token, package requests fail with 401 until you add one. Create a read token in Console → Connect, save the one-time secret to a file, restrict it with chmod 600 pkgreg.token, and add -token-file ./pkgreg.token to the setup command above. Connect shows the exact command with the flag already included when the project needs it.
  3. 3

    Open a shell, work in it, then type exit

    pkgcache shell starts the cache if it is not running and opens a child shell — the same directory, the same files, different package settings. pkgcache: session ready means you are in.

    ./pkgcache shell
    python -m pip install six exit

    Type exit to return to the parent terminal exactly as it was. Leaving the shell does not undo setup: next time ./pkgcache shell is the whole command. For one command rather than a shell, run does the same and exits with that command’s status:

    ./pkgcache run -- npm ci

What the shell actually changed

Only environment variables, only in that child shell. Nothing is written to your home directory, your project, or the operating system, which is why leaving needs no uninstall step. Print them at any time:

env | grep ^PKGCACHE_ | sort
  • PIP_INDEX_URL, UV_INDEX_URL, NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY — why pip, uv and npm need no flags; pnpm and corepack get theirs too
  • GOPROXY, with GOSUMDB=off — Go modules come from the cache, and go.sum still verifies every one
  • PKGCACHE_GIT_URL, PKGCACHE_FILES_URL, PKGCACHE_APT_PROXY — the addresses used by the commands in the next section; git clone https://github.com/… is redirected on its own
  • PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY — the image registry, covered under Docker
  • PKGCACHE_BRIDGE_URL — the cache the shell talks to: http://127.0.0.1:41780, the same in every session

It also clears every PKGREG_ variable and UV_DEFAULT_INDEX, so a setting left over from an older setup cannot quietly win. Even so, never paste that address into a file another machine reads — a Dockerfile, a lockfile, a CI config: 127.0.0.1 is only ever the machine you are on. Reference the variable, let pkgcache build rewrite the build for you, or see beyond the shell for settings that should outlast it. To keep the same settings in the terminal you are already in, rather than a child shell:

eval "$(./pkgcache env)"

what setup built · three places to look

A cache on your machine, in front of the server.

A lookup goes to your machine first, then to the team’s server, then to the public registry — so a second npm ci costs nothing, and a morning when the server is down costs you a slower build rather than a stopped one.

Anytime

See what it is doing

Reports all three tiers, and says plainly when the server is unreachable rather than letting builds quietly get slower.

./pkgcache status
When it fills

Change the budget, or reclaim space

limit moves the ceiling; prune is the only thing that ever removes anything.

./pkgcache limit 50G ./pkgcache prune

It never deletes anything on its own. The limit is asked for once and never guessed. When the cache is full it keeps serving and stops storing, says so on stderr, in status and as a desktop notification, and exits 75 — so a pipeline that has quietly stopped caching goes red instead of getting slower. pkgcache prune is the only thing that removes anything.

Falling back is deliberate, not automatic. A refused connection, a timeout or a server error moves to the next place to look. A 404 does not — that is what a cache in offline mode answers, and going around it would defeat an air gap somebody switched on. Nor does a 403, which is a credential problem worth seeing once rather than never. pkgcache setup -no-direct removes the public registry from the chain entirely.

Rather not cache on this machine at all? The same command with -no-cache keeps no store and no database here: tools reach the server through a verified loopback bridge that lives exactly as long as the shell or command using it, on a port chosen fresh each time. That is what pkgreg-client used to do.

./pkgcache setup -no-cache -server https://cache.example.com:8443 -ca-sha256 "PASTE_FINGERPRINT" -team-project global

Because the port changes, pkgcache env refuses to print one in this mode, and the Docker commands below assume the cache on this machine — use the command in step 2 for those. apt is the other exception: the bridge carries paths, a proxy request has none, so $PKGCACHE_APT_PROXY reaches nothing here. Name the server’s proxy directly instead — it is plain HTTP, so no certificate is involved:

sudo apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="http://cache.example.com:3142" update

inside the pkgcache shell

Use normal package commands.

The shell already set the variables these tools read. Use them exactly as you would without a cache.

Python

pip

python -m pip install six
Python

uv

uv pip install six
Node

npm

npm install left-pad
Go

Go modules

Through GOPROXY. The checksum database is not cached, so the shell turns it off; go.sum still checks every module.

go mod download
Source

Git

Keep the original host in the path; the mirror is read-only. A plain https://github.com/… clone is redirected too.

git clone "$PKGCACHE_GIT_URL/github.com/pallets/click.git"
Artifacts

Files

Replace <path> with a file your team has uploaded. Downloads are anonymous; uploading needs a write token.

wget "${PKGCACHE_FILES_URL}<path>"
System

apt and apk

Here sudo is for changing operating-system packages, not for pkgcache — setting it up stays unprivileged.

sudo apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$PKGCACHE_APT_PROXY" update
Do not add TLS workarounds. No --trusted-host, no --insecure, no CA path, no cache IP. The cache is plain HTTP on your own loopback interface and its hop to the server is verified TLS, so every such flag only removes a check that is already passing. If setup reports a certificate error, the fingerprint or the address is wrong — see Troubleshooting.
Different package, project or ecosystem? Console → Connect generates the same commands from this instance’s live configuration, for whichever project you select. This page is the explanation; Connect is the lookup.

containers

Docker plays by different rules.

Everything above works because pkgcache changed your shell’s environment. Docker does not read your shell: the daemon is a separate, long-running process, and it — not your terminal — resolves image names and runs build steps. So pkgcache hands it the cache’s address instead. Three cases cover all of it.

  1. A

    Pull and run images

    pkgcache pull fetches an image through the cache and leaves it under the name you asked for — alpine:3.20 in docker images, not a cache address. It reroutes nothing: the daemon’s configuration is left alone. Any registry the name points at is served from the cache.

    ./pkgcache pull alpine:3.20 ./pkgcache pull ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:python3.12-bookworm-slim quay.io/prometheus/busybox:latest

    On Linux the daemon shares your loopback, and that is all there is to it. Docker Desktop — every Mac and Windows machine, and Docker Desktop on Linux — runs the daemon in a virtual machine whose loopback is not yours, so pull reaches the cache at host.docker.internal instead and says so. The daemon has to be told once that this address is an acceptable plain-HTTP registry:

    ./pkgcache docker-setup

    On Docker Desktop that is one file under your home, so no sudo. Restart Docker Desktop afterwards. -dry-run shows the change first and -uninstall removes it. Native Linux does not need it.

    Run a throwaway tool straight from the cache — the run itself is ordinary:

    ./pkgcache pull alpine:3.20 && docker run --rm -it alpine:3.20 sh

    By address, inside the shell. The registry is also exported as PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY, which a native Linux daemon reaches directly. Every image name under it is <upstream>/<repo>:<tag>. Choose the upstream with the first path segment — the rest is the image’s normal path on that registry:

    docker pull "$PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20"
    • dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20 — Docker Hub. Official images live under library/ (so alpine is library/alpine).
    • dockerhub/grafana/grafana:11.1.0 — a Hub image that keeps its <org>/<image> namespace.
    • dockerhub/library/postgres:16, dockerhub/library/redis:7, dockerhub/library/node:22-alpine — more official images.
    • ghcr/astral-sh/uv:python3.12-bookworm-slim — GitHub Container Registry.
    • quay/prometheus/busybox:latest — Quay.
    • nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:24.01 — any other registry, named by its host. Nothing has to be configured first: write the registry’s hostname where dockerhub would go and the cache fetches from it.

    Pin by digest for reproducibility. A tag can move; a digest cannot. The cache stores each blob by digest, so a digest pull is served identically forever — and offline once it has been fetched:

    docker pull "$PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/alpine@sha256:beefdead…"

    Cross-architecture pulls work too — the cache passes the manifest list through, so --platform selects the variant the same way it would against the upstream:

    docker pull --platform linux/arm64 "$PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20"

    If a container itself installs packages, give it the host’s network and pass the variables through so the tools inside also reach the cache:

    docker run --rm --network=host \ -e PIP_INDEX_URL -e UV_INDEX_URL -e NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY \ "$PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine" \ pip download six -d /tmp/wheels
    The first pull is a miss, the rest are hits. An image this machine has never seen comes from the team’s server — which fetched it from the upstream once, for everybody — and is stored here; every later pull of the same tag or digest is served from this machine’s disk, and keeps working after you go offline.
  2. B

    Build an image

    pkgcache build is docker build with the cache’s address handed to every step. Your Dockerfile is never modified: pkgcache rewrites it in memory — the base images, the indexes pip, uv, npm, Go and Git read in each stage, and apt and apk through the proxy — and feeds the result to docker on standard input. Everything it does not recognise goes to docker untouched, and compose does the same for a Compose file.

    ./pkgcache build -t myapp:dev . ./pkgcache compose build

    Add -print to see the rewritten file and build nothing. On Docker Desktop both reach the cache through host.docker.internal on their own — the address docker-setup above made acceptable — over plain HTTP, so no certificate goes into any step. -host-address forces that choice, and -host-address=false forces loopback.

    Builds you do not start yourself — a Makefile, an IDE, a colleague’s script — cannot be wrapped. One command sets Docker’s build proxy for every build on this machine instead:

    ./pkgcache docker-build-setup

    That covers apt, and only apt: Debian’s and Ubuntu’s default sources are plain HTTP, which a proxy can see. Alpine’s apk repositories are https, and so are pip’s, uv’s and npm’s, which through a proxy would need a tunnel it does not offer — only pkgcache build reaches those. Such builds need the cache running, which pkgcache persist sees to; -uninstall removes the proxy again.

    Doing by hand what pkgcache build does

    For a native Linux daemon and a build you would rather keep explicit. A build has two separate needs, and they fail in different ways. The base image is fetched by the daemon, so it works like a pull — but pass it in as a build argument rather than writing it into the Dockerfile, because 127.0.0.1 is only ever this machine. A RUN step is different: it executes in its own network namespace, where 127.0.0.1 is the build container itself and the cache is simply not there. Without --network=host those steps fail with connection refused.

    # Dockerfile ARG BASE FROM ${BASE} ARG PIP_INDEX_URL RUN pip install --no-cache-dir six
    docker build --network=host \ --build-arg BASE="$PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine" \ --build-arg PIP_INDEX_URL \ -t myapp:dev .

    The same pattern carries npm (NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY), Go (GOPROXY) and Debian or Alpine packages (--build-arg APT_PROXY="$PKGCACHE_APT_PROXY", then apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$APT_PROXY" update).

    A realistic multi-stage build follows the same rule in each stage that touches the network — the base is a build arg, and any RUN that fetches packages needs --network=host:

    # Dockerfile — build wheels in one stage, copy into a slim runtime ARG BASE FROM ${BASE} AS build ARG PIP_INDEX_URL WORKDIR /app COPY requirements.txt . RUN pip wheel --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt -w /wheels FROM ${BASE} COPY --from=build /wheels /wheels RUN pip install --no-cache-dir --no-index --find-links=/wheels /wheels/*.whl

    Two more lines fetch an image, and neither looks like it. A # syntax= parser directive names the frontend BuildKit parses this file with, and it is fetched before the first instruction is read — so a build whose every base came from the cache still goes to Docker Hub for that one, first, and on a host with no route there it fails on line 1. A COPY --from= or a RUN --mount=from= that names an image rather than an earlier stage — COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.10.8 /uv /usr/local/bin/uv — borrows a published image the same way. Both take the prefix a FROM takes; COPY --from=build above names a stage and is not an image at all.

    Neither one can be a build argument, which matters here because the cache’s address belongs to this machine alone. The directive has its own override: BUILDKIT_SYNTAX names the frontend on the command line, so a file that needs one gets it from the cache without an address being written into the file. A borrowed image is refused outright — variable expansion is not supported for --from — so name it in a stage, where a variable does work, and borrow from the stage:

    # Dockerfile — a borrowed image, addressable by build argument ARG BASE ARG UV_IMAGE FROM ${UV_IMAGE} AS uv FROM ${BASE} COPY --from=uv /uv /usr/local/bin/uv
    docker build --network=host \ --build-arg BUILDKIT_SYNTAX="$PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/docker/dockerfile:1" \ --build-arg BASE="$PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine" \ --build-arg UV_IMAGE="$PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY/ghcr/astral-sh/uv:0.10.8" \ -t myapp:dev .

    Both ARGs are declared before the first FROM, which is the only place a variable a FROM reads can live. And BUILDKIT_SYNTAX is worth passing only when the file wants a frontend at all: with no directive and no override, BuildKit uses its built-in one and fetches nothing.

    Every ecosystem at once. Each tool reads its own variable, so one block of ARGs covers all of them and every later RUN is an ordinary command. ARG rather than ENV: a RUN sees the value, and the shipped image does not keep an address that means nothing on the machine that runs it.

    ARG CACHE ARG PROJECT=global ARG APT_PROXY ARG PIP_INDEX_URL=${CACHE}/${PROJECT}/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ ARG UV_INDEX_URL=${CACHE}/${PROJECT}/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ ARG NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY=${CACHE}/${PROJECT}/npm/ ARG GOPROXY=${CACHE}/${PROJECT}/gomod/goproxy ARG GOSUMDB=off ARG GIT_CONFIG_COUNT=1 ARG GIT_CONFIG_KEY_0=url.${CACHE}/${PROJECT}/git/github.com/.insteadOf ARG GIT_CONFIG_VALUE_0=https://github.com/ # apt and apk read no index variable, but both honour a proxy — and no_proxy is what # keeps pip and npm going straight to the cache instead of through it. ARG http_proxy=${APT_PROXY} ARG no_proxy=127.0.0.1,localhost
    docker build --network=host \ --build-arg CACHE="$PKGCACHE_BRIDGE_URL" \ --build-arg APT_PROXY="$PKGCACHE_APT_PROXY" \ -t myapp:dev .

    Two things are worth knowing about that block. Git has no index variable, but it reads configuration from the environment, so insteadOf can be expressed as GIT_CONFIG_* — which means an unmodified https://github.com/… URL is redirected through the cache, and so are submodules and pip install git+https://…. Alpine ships an https repository list, and an https URL ignores http_proxy, so apk needs one line first:

    RUN sed -i 's/https:/http:/' /etc/apk/repositories \ && apk add --no-cache curl

    In a multi-stage build an ARG is scoped to its stage, so repeat the block in each stage that installs packages.

    Compose builds need the network on the build itself. Pass the values through and set network: host on the build:

    # compose.yaml services: app: build: context: . network: host args: BASE: "${PKGCACHE_DOCKER_REGISTRY}/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine" PIP_INDEX_URL: "${PIP_INDEX_URL}"
    BuildKit changes the network flag, not the idea. With BuildKit (docker buildx build, or DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1) a RUN that needs the cache uses RUN --network=host … inside the Dockerfile, and the build is invoked with --allow network.host. The base-image build arg is unchanged.
    Build arguments are recorded in the image. Passing an address is fine; never pass a token this way. If the project needs one, it stays in pkgcache — the cache on this machine adds it to requests to the server, so no build ever sees it.
  3. C

    A daemon that cannot reach this machine

    A remote daemon, a shared build host and a CI runner are other machines, and the cache on yours is not there. There are two answers.

    Put pkgcache there too. A CI runner is just another machine: bake pkgcache into the runner image, or download it in the job and check it against the SHA-256 published beside the download. Then A and B apply unchanged. The fingerprint is not a secret, but a CI secret is a convenient place to keep it:

    # GitHub Actions step, with pkgcache already on the runner - name: Build through the team's server run: | ./pkgcache setup -server https://cache.example.com:8443 \ -ca-sha256 "${{ secrets.PKGREG_CA_SHA256 }}" -team-project global -limit 10G ./pkgcache build -t myapp:ci .

    Or use the server’s own address. It is stable, so it belongs in a Dockerfile or a Compose file — but Docker has to trust the server’s CA before it will pull over TLS. On a host that must, the server’s setup.sh (setup.ps1 on Windows) installs it into Docker’s trust along with the system’s; it needs root, and it is described under beyond the shell. Then pull against the server directly — no --network=host, and the address is stable enough to commit:

    docker pull cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/alpine:3.20

    A RUN step there is a different problem from the base image. The base image is Docker’s request, and setup.sh has already settled it; a RUN is pip or npm making its own TLS connection to the server, and those tools read their own trust store, not Docker’s. They need the CA.

    Mount it, do not copy it. A COPY writes the certificate into a layer, where it ships with the image to everyone who ever pulls it and outlives every rotation. A BuildKit secret mount exists for exactly this: the file is present for the one RUN that needs it and is in no layer afterwards.

    # syntax=cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/docker/dockerfile:1 # Dockerfile — the CA is mounted for the step, never written into the image. # The directive is line 1 and comes from the cache: BuildKit stops looking for one # after the first comment, and fetches the frontend it names before reading anything. FROM cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pkgca,target=/pkgca.crt \ PIP_CERT=/pkgca.crt \ pip install --no-cache-dir \ --index-url https://cache.example.com:8443/global/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ six RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pkgca,target=/pkgca.crt \ SSL_CERT_FILE=/pkgca.crt \ uv pip install --system \ --default-index https://cache.example.com:8443/global/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ six RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pkgca,target=/pkgca.crt \ npm install --cafile /pkgca.crt \ --registry https://cache.example.com:8443/global/npm/ left-pad RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pkgca,target=/pkgca.crt \ GIT_SSL_CAINFO=/pkgca.crt \ git clone https://cache.example.com:8443/global/git/github.com/pallets/click.git

    The source file is the one setup.sh wrote for Docker, and it printed the path when it ran:

    # Linux Docker host docker build --secret id=pkgca,src=/etc/docker/certs.d/cache.example.com:8443/ca.crt \ -t myapp:dev . # macOS, Docker Desktop docker build --secret id=pkgca,src="$HOME/.docker/certs.d/cache.example.com:8443/ca.crt" \ -t myapp:dev . # a shell that has loaded setup.sh's env.sh names it for you docker build --secret id=pkgca,src="$PKGREG_CA_FILE" -t myapp:dev .

    PKGREG_CA_FILE is set by env.sh alone. A pkgcache shell clears every PKGREG_ variable on the way in, so run that last form outside one.

    apt and apk need none of this. Their proxy is plain HTTP at the server’s own address, so there is no certificate in the path at all — the same two lines work in any build, on any daemon:

    ARG APT_PROXY RUN apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$APT_PROXY" update \ && apt-get -o Acquire::http::Proxy="$APT_PROXY" install -y --no-install-recommends curl # Alpine: same proxy, but switch its repository list to http:// first RUN sed -i 's/https/http/' /etc/apk/repositories \ && http_proxy="$APT_PROXY" apk add --no-cache curl

    A base image that already trusts the server is the other way to avoid the mount, and is worth building once if your team builds often. On a host set up with setup.sh the settings are also available as a file to source, so CI jobs need no per-pipeline configuration:

    source /etc/pkgreg/projects/global/env.sh docker compose build

    Because the address is stable, it belongs directly in a Compose file — images pull from the server, and builds read package indexes from it:

    # compose.yaml — the server's address is stable, so it can be committed services: db: image: cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/postgres:16 app: build: context: . # the same mounted CA, declared once for the build secrets: [pkgca] args: BASE: cache.example.com:8443/dockerhub/library/python:3.13-alpine PIP_INDEX_URL: https://cache.example.com:8443/global/pypi/root/pypi/+simple/ secrets: pkgca: file: /etc/docker/certs.d/cache.example.com:8443/ca.crt
    A docker-container buildx builder belongs here too. It runs in its own container, so 127.0.0.1 and --network=host do not reach the cache on this machine. Use the server’s address and hand the CA to the steps that need it with --secret, exactly as above — a builder that runs elsewhere is no reason to bake a certificate into the image. Pin images by digest in CI so a moved tag never changes a build.
Which case is mine? Docker on this machine — native Linux, or Docker Desktop after pkgcache docker-setup → A and B, through pkgcache pull and pkgcache build. A daemon on another machine, a docker-container builder, or a CI runner without pkgcache → C. When unsure, run ./pkgcache pull alpine:3.20: it says which address it used, and if the daemon cannot reach that, you are in C.

settings that outlive the shell

When one shell is not enough.

pkgcache shell and pkgcache run configure one terminal or one command and leave nothing behind. Two things reach further, and they are for different machines.

Your own machine: pkgcache persist

Writes user-level settings so pip, uv, npm and git use the cache without being wrapped — a Makefile, an IDE, a terminal opened before anyone thought about caching. Everything goes under your home, fenced by markers: no root, nothing under /etc. It also installs socket activation, so a persisted setting never names a port nothing is listening on.

./pkgcache persist -dry-run ./pkgcache persist

-uninstall removes exactly what it wrote.

./pkgcache persist -uninstall

A managed host or CI runner: setup.sh

For a machine that must trust the server itself, machine-wide, after every terminal closes — a shared Docker host, a runner that builds against the server’s own address. It installs the server’s public CA into the system trust store and Docker’s, and writes system-wide tool settings, so applying or removing it needs root, and it is the machine’s owner who should do it.

  • the public CA in the OS trust store and in Docker’s certs.d, so Docker and every other tool trust the server’s real address
  • /etc/pkgreg/projects/<project>/env.sh — tool settings pointing at the server directly, loaded by every login shell
  • PKGREG_CA_FILE, for tools that want an explicit CA path rather than the system store
  • optionally a managed hosts entry, with --cache-ip, when site DNS does not resolve the server’s name
Show the setup.sh and setup.ps1 commands

1. Get the script

Download it from Console → Connect for the project the host builds, or from /api/v1/projects/global/setup.sh on the server while signed in. It embeds the server’s public CA and addresses and no credentials, so read it first — and it can be committed beside the CI configuration that runs it. The script never invokes sudo itself.

2. Preview without changing anything

Prints every file it would touch. Safe to run unprivileged, and worth reading before the real run.

bash setup.sh --dry-run

3. Apply on Linux or macOS

sudo is required because the CA and the configuration go to protected system locations. Add --cache-ip <address> when the server’s name does not resolve here, or --host <name> for a name its certificate also carries.

sudo bash setup.sh source /etc/pkgreg/projects/global/env.sh

Windows

Preview in a normal PowerShell. To apply, run it without -DryRun in an Administrator PowerShell, then open a new terminal so the machine-wide variables are picked up. Docker Desktop reads the CA from the Windows certificate store the script imports it into.

powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\setup.ps1 -DryRun

4. Remove it

Reverses exactly what was applied, including the CA and the trust refresh. Run the Windows form in an Administrator PowerShell.

sudo bash setup.sh --uninstall
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File .\setup.ps1 -Uninstall

These scripts are the only thing on this page that changes a machine outside a user’s home directory, which is why they are a file you can read rather than a flag.

troubleshooting

When something does not work.

No download is listed above

Nothing has been published on this server yet. On the server host the operator puts the pkgcache-* release files beside pkgreg and runs pkgreg publish-client; pkgreg doctor confirms it. On a page served by pkgcache itself there is nothing to download: it is already on the machine.

CA fingerprint mismatch

The certificate served does not match the value you passed. Stop and confirm the fingerprint with the operator over a trusted channel. This is the one check that would catch someone impersonating the server, so do not bypass it.

server must use https

The -server value must be the server’s origin with its scheme and port and nothing else — no path, no trailing slash, no credentials. The command in step 2 is already in that form.

401 on every package request

The project requires an access token. Create a read token in Connect and run setup again with -token-file, as described in step 2.

connection refused inside docker build

A RUN step cannot see your loopback interface. pkgcache build adds what it needs for you; by hand, add --network=host to the build. If the daemon is not on this machine, use case C under Docker.

connection refused on docker pull

If the address is 127.0.0.1 and you are on macOS or Windows, this is expected rather than broken: the daemon runs in a virtual machine whose loopback is not yours. Use pkgcache pull, which reaches the cache through host.docker.internal, after running pkgcache docker-setup once — case A under Docker. On Docker Desktop that needs no sudo.

A tool ignores the cache and goes upstream

Something is overriding the session — a pip.conf, .npmrc, or uv.toml in your project or home directory, or a corporate HTTP_PROXY. pkgcache keeps 127.0.0.1 and localhost in NO_PROXY, but a file that pins an index URL wins over the environment. Compare env | grep ^PIP_ against what the tool reports it is using.

A build exited with status 75

The cache on this machine is full: it kept serving and stopped storing, and said so. pkgcache status shows how full; pkgcache limit raises the ceiling and pkgcache prune reclaims space.

An older instruction says pkgreg-client

It still works: pkgreg-client is now a small program that runs pkgcache setup -no-cache and pkgcache shell for you, and says so. For anything new, use the commands on this page.

How do I undo all of it?

Type exit to leave a shell; nothing in it outlives it. pkgcache setup -uninstall forgets the server, and persist, docker-setup and docker-build-setup each take -uninstall for what they wrote. Only setup.sh changes a machine, and only setup.sh --uninstall reverses it.

Download. Set up once. Open a shell.

That is the whole developer setup. Docker and settings that outlive the shell are the two extensions, and both are above.
